summary: Provides supporting documentation to advance PIM-SM from Experimental status to Proposed Standard. It is an informational analysis supporting that move.

eli5.summary: This is a report card showing a multicast method works well enough to be promoted from a trial to a proper standard.

subtitle: Requirements checklist for advancing PIM-SM from Experimental to Standard.

tldr.problem: PIM-SM was an experimental multicast routing protocol that had been deployed in networks but needed a formal standardization review.
tldr.mechanism: This document checks whether PIM-SM meets all the requirements for advancing to Proposed Standard status, evaluating its specification quality, implementation maturity, testing evidence, security architecture and authentication mechanisms.
tldr.outcome: PIM-SM met all requirements and advanced to Proposed Standard in 2006. The protocol is now a mature standard for efficient multicast routing across wide-area networks.

facts.label: Primary testing approach
facts.value: XORP state machine testing, Cisco production deployment, Procket interop

today: PIM-SM is now an Internet Standard, successfully advanced from Experimental status. It is widely deployed in service provider networks for efficient multicast routing. Multiple implementations continue to interoperate, and the protocol remains suitable for routing multicast groups across wide-area and inter-domain networks.

sections.title: What This Document Does
sections.content:
RFC 4602 provides the formal supporting documentation needed to advance Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode (PIM-SM) from IETF Experimental status to Proposed Standard status. PIM-SM is a routing protocol used to deliver data to multiple recipients (multicast) across wide-area networks. The protocol was first published in 1997 and 1998 as Experimental, and later completely rewritten with a more rigorous specification.

This document verifies that the new specification meets all of RFC 1264's requirements for routing protocols seeking Proposed Standard advancement, including requirements for clear documentation, implementations, testing evidence, and security architecture.
sections.eli5: This is a checklist showing that a multicast method has been written clearly, tested by different teams, and is safe enough to be promoted to official standard status.

sections.title: Requirements from RFC 1264
sections.content:
RFC 1264 defines seven requirements for routing protocols seeking Proposed Standard status:

  • Documentation: The specification must be clear and comprehensive. The new PIM-SM specification removes all known ambiguities from earlier versions and fully specifies the protocol operation.
  • Management: Management tools must exist. PIM has a Management Information Base (MIB) standardized in RFC 2934, used in production for several years.
  • Security: An explicit security architecture is required. PIM-SM specifies security using IPsec authentication headers for data integrity and origin authentication of protocol messages.
  • Authentication: Authentication mechanisms are defined. PIM uses IPsec's authentication header with administrator-configured algorithms and keys.
  • Suitability: The protocol must be suitable for its stated purpose. PIM-SM efficiently routes multicast groups across wide-area and inter-domain networks using underlying unicast routing for path information.
sections.eli5: The standard checklist requires: a clear instruction manual, management tools, safety features, authentication to prove who sent messages, and proof it actually works for what it claims to do.

sections.title: Known Implementations
sections.content:
At least four independent implementations of the new PIM-SM specification exist, plus more than six implementations of the previous version. The four new implementations are:

  • XORP: An open-source implementation available since December 2002, written by Pavlin Radoslavov (not an author of the specification), starting from scratch.
  • Cisco IOS/IOX: Production implementations by Cisco Systems for both IPv4 and IPv6, initially written by Isidor Kouvelas. The new specification is backward compatible with the old specification, allowing existing implementations to be compliant with minimal changes.
  • Infosys Technologies: A shared-tree implementation used in commercial products, covering key features like Hello messages, DR election, join/prune messages, join suppression, and prune override.
  • Procket Networks: An implementation written from scratch and later acquired by Cisco, showing the protocol's commercial viability.
sections.eli5: Four different teams, some who never read the specification before, wrote working versions of PIM-SM. That shows the spec is clear enough for real implementations.

sections.title: Testing Evidence
sections.content:
Multiple implementations have undergone extensive testing:

  • Cisco Testing: Laboratory testing and production deployment testing shows interoperability with earlier versions of PIM-SM protocol implementations.
  • XORP Testing: Thorough internal testing using packet generators and observers. Tests follow the protocol specification closely, with separate tests for each state machine event. Major tested features include data forwarding, neighbor discovery, DR election, Register messages, Join/Prune messages across multiple states ((*,*,RP), (*,G), (S,G), and (S,G,rpt)), Assert messages, and the Bootstrap mechanism. Final tests confirmed the implementation behaves as specified.
  • Procket Networks: Deployed in research and service provider networks with demonstrated interoperability with Cisco and Juniper implementations.
sections.eli5: The implementations were tested by sending them different network messages and checking they responded correctly. All tests passed, showing the recipe really works in practice.

sections.title: Security and Authentication
sections.content:
PIM-SM uses IPsec's authentication header (AH) for data integrity protection and groupwise data origin authentication of protocol messages. Network administrators configure the specific authentication algorithm and parameters, including which algorithm to use and which key to use. The security considerations section of the protocol specification outlines the threats from receiving forged PIM messages, such as false routing information that could disrupt multicast delivery.

The protocol's backward compatibility with earlier versions means existing deployments can continue operating while benefiting from improved security in new implementations.
sections.eli5: PIM protects itself by requiring messages to be authenticated with a special signature, so routers know messages are really from trusted PIM routers and not fake.
